name: Emeka Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in-house at a snack company, the crisps and oat bar kind, and I sit on the brand team for the oat bars. Most mornings start with a stand-up at nine, then I'm writing: packaging copy, social posts, the little lines on the back of the box that people read while the kettle boils. Afternoons are briefs to the design agency, comments on artwork and a lot of chasing legal about whether we can say "wholesome".

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the writing, honestly, finding the one line that makes a bar of oats feel like a small treat. What wears me out is the approval chain: six people sign off a forty-word caption, and by the end it says nothing. I still write first drafts in a paper notebook on the train, which my team finds very funny, and I've never touched the AI writing tools the agency keeps showing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that one sounds like a relief. The agency keeps pitching us AI tools that write captions, and half the time the output is bland anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. At work I'd tell the team we can stop pretending every new tool is going to rewrite marketing, and get back to making good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad, because I'm not someone who likes learning a new system every quarter. My job's secure, the pay is good for my level, and Ines (my partner) is a nurse, so between us the money is steady. The only thing I'd still worry about is that the company keeps cutting the brand team's budget whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I do now. I'd keep writing, keep putting a chunk of my pay into savings each month, and keep going to the marketing workers' group meetings, the one a few of us joined last year to push for fair freelance rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, which isn't my best side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned budget cuts. Is that a worry already, before any AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. Last spring they didn't replace a colleague who left, so I picked up the granola account on top of the oat bars, and nobody talked about pay. With ten months of savings I'm not scared, but I'd still raise it at the workers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be talking to about all this outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, mostly, over dinner. She'd laugh, because her ward has had a new computer system every year and none of them saved her a single minute.

say: I'd tell the team the **AI hype** was overblown and we should get back to making good work.
I'd say good copy still comes from **people who care**, not from a caption generator.
think: Privately I'd feel **relieved**, because I don't want to learn a new tool every quarter.
My job and the **household money** feel secure, with Ines on a steady nursing wage.
The real pressure is **budget cuts**, which were happening before AI came up.
do: Keep **writing drafts** by hand and running the oat bar and granola accounts as now.
Keep putting **part of each payslip** into savings, on top of the ten months already saved.
Raise the **unpaid extra account** at the marketing workers' group meetings.
feel: **Calm** overall, with a little **smugness** he admits isn't his best side.
S0.quote: Last spring they didn't replace a colleague who left, so I picked up the granola account on top of the oat bars, and nobody talked about pay.
fieldNote: He frames AI as **hype** and is visibly glad to be proven right.
His one real grievance is **workload creep**, which predates AI and which he links to unions.
Strong savings and a partner in **nursing** make this world feel safe to him.

steps.text: Keep writing oat bar and granola copy the way he does now
Keep adding part of each payslip to the ten months already saved
Raise unpaid extra accounts at the marketing workers' group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's much closer to home. Writing, checking, planning, answering customers: that's basically my whole job description read back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on this, written down, before anyone decides the brand team can be halved. Online I'd probably post something angry about companies using AI to cut jobs and calling it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I'm average at my job, I'm the one who refuses to use the tools, and my manager Gillian already calls me the analogue guy. If the team shrinks from seven to four, I can see exactly how that meeting goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get the workers' group to push for a written agreement on AI at our company, with notice before any role is cut. I'd stop the extras, like the ski trip Ines and I were planning, and move another few thousand into savings. I'd probably sit through the AI training, grumbling, because refusing would just make me the obvious name on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a knot in my stomach. I'm angry, but under the anger I'm a bit scared, because I don't really know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit through the training. Would you actually use the tools afterwards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the boring bits, maybe, like resizing a caption for six platforms. But I'd keep the ideas and the first draft for myself, because if a machine writes those, what am I being paid for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are plenty of marketing jobs nearby. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps less than it sounds. Every brand team in the city would be shrinking at the same time, so I'd be one of a hundred copywriters chasing the same three openings.

say: I'd say companies need **written rules** on AI before anyone halves the brand team.
Online I'd call it **cutting jobs** and dressing it up as efficiency.
think: I think I'd be **one of the first** to go, as the average one who refuses the tools.
Plenty of **nearby jobs** won't help much if every brand team shrinks at once.
do: Push the workers' group for a **written AI agreement** with notice before any role is cut.
Cancel the **ski trip** and move a few thousand more into savings.
Sit through the **AI training** and use it only for resizing captions.
feel: A **knot** in his stomach: anger on top, with **fear** underneath it.
S1.quote: Writing, checking, planning, answering customers: that's basically my whole job description read back to me.
fieldNote: His **self-assessment** is blunt: average, resistant, and likely first on the list.
He'd use **collective action** first and the AI tools only grudgingly.
He sees the **local job market** shrinking for everyone at once, not just for him.

steps.text: Push the workers' group for a written AI agreement at the snack company
Move a few thousand more into savings this year
Cancel the ski trip planned with his partner
Use the AI tool only for resizing captions across platforms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a plan, that's a cliff. Robots three years later doesn't matter to me at all, because there's nothing hands-on in my job except carrying samples to a photo shoot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this has to be stopped or slowed, and that the companies making it should pay for what it breaks. I'd be at every protest, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen to vote for whoever promises to tax it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone, probably within a year of it arriving. Brand copy and campaign plans are exactly the thinking work it does best. The only thing that keeps me sane is Ines, because nursing is hands-on and she'd have about three more years than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food and keep the whole ten months untouched. I'd look straight away at the nursing support worker course Ines keeps mentioning, because it's hands-on and buys me a few years. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income, because I don't see another way through for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'm 27, and the thing I trained for would be over before I'm 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ines that I might be the one at home for a while and she might be carrying us, and that I hate that. Then we'd probably sit there working out how long ten months really lasts on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Could you really retrain that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that scares me more than the money does. I've avoided every new tool for five years, and now I'd have to start a whole new trade with my hands.

say: I'd say AGI must be **slowed or taxed**, and the companies behind it should pay for the damage.
I'd tell everyone to **vote** for whoever promises to tax it, and turn up to protests.
think: I think my **job is gone** within about a year of AGI arriving.
My partner's **nursing job** gives the household roughly three more years than mine.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and keep the ten months of savings untouched.
Look into the **nursing support worker** course his partner keeps mentioning.
Join **basic income** campaigns and protests against the companies behind AGI.
feel: **Sick** at the thought that his training is over before he turns **30**.
Scared he **can't retrain** fast, after years of avoiding anything new.
S2.quote: I'm 27, and the thing I trained for would be over before I'm 30.
fieldNote: He sees **no hands-on part** of his job, so the robot delay means nothing to him.
His household plan rests on his partner's **nursing wage**, which he finds hard to accept.
His deepest fear is his own **resistance to change**, more than the money.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and leave the savings untouched
Apply for the nursing support worker course his partner suggested
Vote and campaign for a tax on AGI and a basic income
Join protests against the companies building AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it's different from two. I'd be 32 when it lands, which feels like enough time to do something, if I actually start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: tax it, regulate it, protect workers. But I'd also say to friends that this one gives us a few years, so let's not waste them pretending it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think marketing is over for me by 2031 either way. The difference is that with five years I could finish a proper qualification while I'm still being paid, instead of scrambling. If I'm sensible, I'd be out before the cuts come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a part-time healthcare course in the evenings, probably the support worker route, and keep my day job. I'd put more into savings, aiming for a year and a half. I'd keep pushing the workers' group for decent redundancy terms, so whoever's left at the end isn't thrown out with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy in my stomach, but less sick than the fast one. More like dread with a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why healthcare and not something closer to what you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because anything close to what I do now is screen work, and screen work is exactly what goes first. Ines says care work is hard on the body, but at least a person has to be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive about three years later, around 2034. Does that worry you for the new path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. But I'd rather have three more years of work with people than none at all, and I'd hope by then there are rules about robots in care.

say: I'd keep saying **tax and regulate** AGI and protect the people it displaces.
I'd tell friends **five years** is time we shouldn't waste pretending it won't happen.
think: I think marketing is **over for me** by 2031, whatever I do.
Five years means I could **finish a qualification** while still being paid.
do: Start a **part-time healthcare course** in the evenings while keeping the day job.
Build savings towards a year and a half of **household costs**.
Push the workers' group for **decent redundancy** terms for whoever is left.
feel: Less sick than the fast picture: **dread with a timetable**.
S3.quote: Anything close to what I do now is screen work, and screen work is exactly what goes first.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his panic into a **retraining plan** he can picture.
He picks **care work** because a person has to be in the room, accepting it is hard.
He still trusts **unions and rules** to soften the robot wave around 2034.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening healthcare support worker course next year
Save towards a year and a half of household costs
Push the workers' group for decent redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole career stage, so it feels less like a cliff and more like a slope I can see the bottom of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to get the rules right, so let's actually do it: a tax on AI profits, retraining paid for properly, and unions at the table. I'd be less angry in public and more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably do nothing for the first year or two, which is my worst habit. I know myself: if the deadline is far away, I'll keep writing oat bar copy and tell myself I'll start next year. The job still goes eventually, so I'd need someone to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Realistically, I'd keep my job, keep saving, and help the workers' group set up a proper training fund with the company. I'd tell myself to start a course by year three at the latest. Ines and I would probably still buy a small flat, because with ten years we could pay a good chunk off first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but uneasy underneath. It's the kind of worry that sits in the back of your head while you get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a flat. Isn't that risky if your job goes by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but rent is a risk too. If we paid off a big piece before 2036, we'd need less coming in later, and that feels like the safest thing I can do with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, instead of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the diary and someone checking on me, honestly. If the workers' group ran a course with the company paying for half, I'd be on it, because I hate wasting free money more than I hate change.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to get the rules right: an AI tax, paid retraining, unions at the table.
I'd be **more organised** and less angry in public than in the faster pictures.
think: I know I'd probably **put off** acting for a year or two, which is my worst habit.
The **job still goes** by 2036, so I'd need someone pushing me to start.
do: Help the workers' group set up a **company training fund** in the first year.
Buy a **small flat** with his partner and pay a big chunk off before 2036.
Set a deadline to **start a course** by year three at the latest.
feel: **Calmer**, with an **uneasy** worry sitting in the back of his head.
S4.quote: If the deadline is far away, I'll keep writing oat bar copy and tell myself I'll start next year.
fieldNote: He's honest that a **long deadline** feeds his habit of putting things off.
He'd lean on **collective structures**, like a training fund, to make himself act.
Buying a **flat** is his way of lowering future costs before the job goes.

steps.text: Help the workers' group set up a company-paid training fund
Buy a small flat with his partner and overpay the mortgage
Start a retraining course by the third year at the latest
Keep the oat bar job unchanged for the first year or two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with nothing hands-on in my job and no head start on anything else. What would help is time and money to retrain, paid for by the companies that profit, and a basic income for the gap so I'm not living off Ines for years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how much of this is about pride. If I'm honest, losing the job wouldn't hurt me as much as being told a machine writes better than me. Writing is the one thing I've always been good at.

headlineQuote: Losing the job wouldn't hurt me as much as being told a machine writes better than me.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old copywriter** on a snack company's oat bar team, with ten months saved and a nurse partner.
He writes first drafts **by hand**, has never used AI tools and calls his own skill average.
He leans on **unions and regulation** first and blames companies that cut jobs and call it efficiency.
He moves from **calm** in the plateau to **alarmed** at two-year AGI, then towards retraining in healthcare.
He admits a long deadline would make him **put things off**, so he wants structures that push him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all **screen** work with no head start elsewhere.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** funded by the companies that profit, and a **basic income** for the gap.
